name: Ocean alkalinity ship
subtitle: a ship that makes the sea absorb carbon

effects.effect: graphene lets protons through but stops every atom and molecule
a current splits water into hydrogen and oxygen
a system at balance shifts to resist any push

effect: graphene lets protons through but stops every atom and molecule
how: The sea already holds most of the carbon we have emitted, and it would take far more if it were slightly less acidic. On board, a current splits seawater while a one-atom carbon sheet lets only the hydrogen's bare protons cross, cleanly separating an acid stream from an alkaline one; the alkaline water goes overboard, and the sea, pushed out of balance, pulls carbon dioxide out of the air for months to restore it. The acid is neutralised below deck against crushed volcanic rock.
obstacle: Moving enough rock and water to matter means a fleet, and no regulator yet knows how to permit changing the chemistry of open ocean.
why: A proton-only membrane makes clean acid-base splitting of seawater practical at ship scale.
real: Electrochemical ocean alkalinity enhancement has been field-tested from shore (Ebb Carbon's bipolar-membrane prototype at Sequim, 47,000 gallons discharged) and MIT has proposed membrane-free electrochemical 'ocean-scrubbing' ships at lab scale, but no vessel-mounted electrochemical alkalinity system exists; the one ship-mounted ocean-CDR system in development (Calcarea) uses limestone, not electrodialysis.
